articles.title: Myanmar Joins ASEAN Tourism Talks as Human Rights Crisis Shadows Investment - eTurboNews
articles.summary: Myanmar Joins ASEAN Tourism Talks as Human Rights Crisis Shadows Investment  eTurboNews
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — Myanmar joined ASEAN tourism leaders at the ASEAN Tourism Ministers’ Retreat in Manila on 29 September 2026, as Southeast Asian governments discussed sustainable tourism investment, infrastructure and regional resilience. Myanmar’s delegation was led by H.E. Daw Ei Ei Tin, Ambassador/Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of the Embassy of Myanmar in Manila.
Held at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the retreat was chaired by Philippine Tourism Undersecretary Verna Buensuceso and attended by tourism ministers, deputy ministers and ASEAN representatives. The meeting comes as Myanmar remains affected by armed conflict, displacement and serious human-rights concerns, putting questions over tourism safety, investment, military-linked commercial interests and the beneficiaries of tourism revenue alongside ASEAN’s efforts to promote sustainable tourism growth.
A central topic at the Manila retreat was the development of the ASEAN Sustainable and Resilient Tourism Investment Outlook, an initiative intended to mobilise quality and sustainable investment, strengthen tourism infrastructure, improve the resilience of destinations and increase competitiveness across Southeast Asia.
The retreat was held alongside the ASEAN Tourism Investment Showcase, where participating ASEAN member states and relevant stakeholders exchanged views and presented opportunities for investment in the region’s tourism sector.
The wider objective is to strengthen ASEAN as an interconnected and competitive tourism region while encouraging investment capable of withstanding economic shocks, environmental pressures, geopolitical uncertainty and other disruptions.
For most ASEAN destinations, that discussion centers on attracting capital, improving connectivity and encouraging travelers to explore destinations beyond established tourism centers.
For Myanmar, however, those objectives intersect with a far more difficult political, security, humanitarian and human-rights environment.
The 29 September meeting brought together ministers, deputy ministers and senior officials responsible for tourism from ASEAN member states, as well as representatives of the ASEAN Secretariat.
Myanmar was represented by a delegation headed by H.E. Daw Ei Ei Tin, Ambassador/Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of the Embassy of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar in Manila.
The retreat was chaired by H.E. Ms. Verna Buensuceso, Undersecretary of the Department of Tourism of the Philippines.
The Deputy Secretary-General of ASEAN and his delegation also participated.
The gathering formed part of ASEAN’s wider effort to coordinate tourism policy as Southeast Asian destinations confront changing international travel patterns, economic uncertainty, climate risks and geopolitical tensions.
Myanmar remains an ASEAN member, but its position within the organisation has been complicated since the military seized power on 1 February 2021.
ASEAN responded to the crisis with its Five-Point Consensus, calling for an end to violence, constructive dialogue among the parties, humanitarian assistance and diplomatic engagement.
ASEAN leaders have subsequently acknowledged a lack of substantive progress in implementing the consensus.
Myanmar’s appearance at a sector-specific gathering such as the Tourism Ministers’ Retreat therefore needs to be distinguished from ASEAN’s handling of Myanmar’s political representation at its highest-level meetings.
The Manila gathering demonstrates that Myanmar continues to participate in areas of ASEAN technical and economic cooperation even as the organisation continues to confront the unresolved political and humanitarian crisis in the country.
Myanmar possesses some of Southeast Asia’s most significant cultural and natural tourism assets.
They include the ancient temples of Bagan, Yangon’s religious and colonial heritage, Inle Lake, beaches, mountain landscapes and the Myeik Archipelago.
Before years of political instability and conflict, Myanmar had been attempting to establish itself as one of Southeast Asia’s emerging international tourism destinations.
That development has been severely disrupted.
The military takeover in February 2021 triggered widespread resistance and an armed conflict that subsequently expanded across large parts of the country.
Millions of people have been displaced internally or across international borders, while fighting and insecurity continue to affect numerous regions.
Several foreign governments maintain extensive travel warnings for Myanmar because of armed conflict, arbitrary detention, political violence and unpredictable security conditions.
Tourism nevertheless continues on a reduced scale, including domestic travel and some international arrivals.
This creates a stark contrast with the investment agenda discussed in Manila: ASEAN is considering new destinations, stronger infrastructure and tourism investment through 2030 while significant areas of Myanmar remain affected by conflict or difficult to access safely.
The relationship between tourism and human rights in Myanmar extends beyond the immediate question of whether foreign visitors can travel safely.
One of the central questions is where tourism money ultimately goes.
Concerns about tourism revenues and military-linked commercial interests predate the February 2021 takeover.
A United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission investigated the extensive commercial interests of Myanmar’s armed forces, including the military-linked conglomerates Myanmar Economic Holdings Limited (MEHL) and Myanmar Economic Corporation (MEC).
The UN investigation identified military commercial interests across numerous economic sectors, including links to the hotel and tourism industry.
It called for enhanced human-rights due diligence and urged businesses and consumers to avoid commercial relationships that could financially benefit military-controlled enterprises.
This does not mean that every hotel, restaurant, tour operator or tourism business in Myanmar is associated with the military.
That distinction is important.
Tourism can also provide income directly to ordinary people — including independent guides, drivers, restaurant employees, craftspeople, family-owned accommodation providers and local communities — many of whom are themselves struggling with the economic consequences of conflict.
The human-rights question surrounding Myanmar tourism is therefore more complex than simply asking whether tourists should or should not visit.
Relevant questions include who owns tourism businesses, who ultimately receives travellers’ money, how tourism land was acquired, how workers are treated, whether communities participate in decisions and whether commercial arrangements benefit entities associated with human-rights abuses.
Any discussion of responsible or sustainable tourism in Myanmar also exists against the background of the continuing human-rights situation involving the Rohingya and other ethnic minorities.
The Rohingya crisis, mass displacement and continuing conflict in Rakhine State have been the subject of extensive scrutiny by United Nations bodies and international human-rights organisations.
This becomes particularly relevant when tourism development involves land, infrastructure or investment in conflict-affected areas.
Projects promoted as sustainable cannot necessarily be assessed solely according to environmental credentials or financial returns.
Questions surrounding land ownership, displacement, community consent, security and the distribution of economic benefits are also relevant to assessing the sustainability of tourism development.
These conditions create difficult questions for international tourism investors.
Myanmar’s tourism potential remains substantial. Years of reduced international tourism have also left many people working in hospitality and associated sectors in need of income.
Investment could potentially support employment, independent businesses, cultural preservation and community livelihoods.
But investment in a conflict-affected country requires considerably greater scrutiny than an ordinary hotel, resort or tourism development project.
Investors need to understand who owns the land on which projects are built, who their local partners are, where payments ultimately go and whether commercial partners have connections with sanctioned, military-controlled or military-associated entities.
Similar considerations can apply to international tour operators when selecting hotels, transportation providers, destination-management companies and other suppliers.
This is where the language used at the ASEAN meeting — particularly “quality and sustainable investment” — becomes especially significant.
In Myanmar, quality tourism investment cannot realistically be assessed only by the amount of capital invested, the number of hotel rooms constructed or the number of tourists attracted.
Its wider social and human-rights consequences also matter.
The Manila retreat placed sustainability and resilience at the centre of ASEAN’s future tourism strategy.
Myanmar tests how broadly those concepts are interpreted.
A tourism development can reduce plastic consumption, conserve water and improve energy efficiency while still raising serious sustainability concerns if land was obtained without meaningful community consent or if revenue ultimately reaches entities implicated in abuses.
Conversely, carefully structured tourism can potentially provide livelihoods, support independent businesses, preserve cultural heritage and generate income for communities facing severe economic hardship.
For investors, this means environmental due diligence alone may be insufficient.
Companies considering tourism projects in Myanmar also need to examine ownership structures, business partners, land arrangements, financial beneficiaries, sanctions exposure and possible connections with military-controlled or military-associated entities.

JAKARTA – An excavator smashed through roofs and walls, leaving piles of rubble where a cluster of “luxury villas” stood inside an Indonesian prison amid allegations that selected inmates received special treatment, as the authorities said an investigation had preliminarily found an abuse of authority.
Ten buildings at Cibinong Class 2A prison in Bogor, West Java, were demolished on Sept 30 after lawmakers and the prison authorities agreed to tear them down, saying they were not state assets and had been built without permits along a riverbank where construction was prohibited.
Footage showed the excavator tearing through the white-painted buildings as roofs and ceiling frames collapsed. Before the demolition, officers removed mattresses, sofas, cupboards, refrigerators and televisions and loaded them onto trucks.
The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections classified the case as a serious disciplinary violation that could lead to sanctions ranging from demotion to dismissal. “The preliminary conclusion is that there was an abuse of authority,” ministry inspector-general Rudi Setiawan told a press conference at Cibinong prison on Sept 30.
The demolition came a week after Indonesia’s national Ombudsman found inmates apparently living outside their regular prison blocks in unusually well-equipped residences during a surprise inspection on Sept 23.
Inspectors had initially sought to enter the regular cell blocks but were refused entry despite presenting an official assignment letter. They instead investigated a fenced-off area about 100m away and found more than 10 residential units resembling homestays, terraced houses and villas.
One occupant told inspectors he was an inmate. The Ombudsman later said some residences housed several inmates and others just one, while one inmate acknowledged paying to stay there. Investigators have yet to establish how much was paid or to whom.
Five senior prison officials, including the warden and head of prison security, were suspended on Sept 26.
At a parliamentary hearing two days later, Corrections director-general Mashudi, who goes by one name, maintained that the buildings were official residences for prison staff but acknowledged that 13 of 16 were not registered in the government’s state asset system. Of those 13, 10 were identified as outside the ministry’s assets and demolished on Sept 30.
Rudi said investigators were trying to establish who had allowed people to occupy the buildings.
“As the Ombudsman saw, some of these buildings were indeed occupied or inhabited, as indicated by photographs. We have obtained some information about who was there, and we are following up on who allowed this to happen and other matters,” he said.
Investigators were also examining the procurement of a gym and a room intended for a golf simulator. Rudi said the simulator had not been completed, with only carpeting done.
Officials questioned the suspended warden Wisnu Hani Putranto again on Sept 29 and confronted him with information obtained during earlier questioning, Rudi said.
He said investigators had yet to determine who was responsible and needed to examine other accounts and evidence before reaching final conclusions.
Lawmakers also sought to ensure evidence was preserved before the demolition.
“Everything has been examined, recorded, photographed and inventoried,” said Sugiat Santoso, deputy chairman of the House of Representatives’ Commission 13, during an inspection of the prison on Sept 30. He said Commission 13, which oversees regulatory reform and human rights, also called for unauthorised buildings and facilities at prisons across Indonesia to be removed or brought into compliance so that inmates receive equal treatment.
On Sept 25, Sugiat had described the units as “luxury villas” suspected of being used by inmates.
The ministry is expected to present further findings to Commission 13 at another parliamentary hearing on Oct 5.

articles.title: Digital platform adds new channel for Vietnamese exporters to reach global buyers - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Digital platform adds new channel for Vietnamese exporters to reach global buyers  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNS/VNA) - Vietnamese exporters will have a new digital channel to connect with overseas buyers as Ho Chi Minh City combines online business matching with traditional trade promotion. 
 
 The Expo Platform, developed by the Centre for Technical Support and Sustainable Development under the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade and Arobid Technology JSC, was launched on September 29 as part of preparations for the 2026 Outstanding Vietnamese Export Products Fair. 
 
 The platform is scheduled to go live on October 20, allowing businesses and cooperatives to create digital booths, showcase products and communicate with potential buyers beyond the physical exhibition. 
 
 The initiative comes as Ho Chi Minh City seeks to diversify export markets and strengthen local businesses' participation in global value chains. The city's exports reached more than 65.8 billion USD in the first eight months of 2026, up 7.82% year-on-year, according to the city’s Department of Industry and Trade. 
 
 The department said market diversification, better use of free trade agreements and improvements in product quality and standards would remain important to export growth. 
 
 The export fair, taking place from October 22–24 at WTC EXPO International Exhibition Centre, will feature 750 booths covering major export sectors including textiles and footwear, food and agricultural products, Halal food, wood products, handicrafts, household equipment and hand tools. 
 
 It will also introduce an “on-site export centre”, connecting international buyers directly with businesses, factories and production areas. 
 
 According to Le Van Danh, deputy director of the HCM City Department of Industry and Trade, the combination of direct meetings, production-site visits and digital connectivity will give buyers more opportunities to assess Vietnamese suppliers. 
 
 “Instead of only bringing businesses to display their products, the programme aims to bring international buyers, procurement groups and distribution systems directly to production areas,” Danh said. 
 
 So far, 21 delegations comprising 103 buyers have registered for the event. They come from the US, France, Canada, Hungary, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Taiwan (China), China, Cambodia, Myanmar, Dubai, Thailand, the Republic of Korea, Japan and other markets. 
 
 Data becomes part of export promotion 
 
 For exporters, however, putting products online is only one part of the process. 
 
 Tran Van Chin, chairman of Arobid Technology JSC, said the quality of digital information would be critical to helping buyers find and assess suppliers. 
 
 Company profiles and product information need to be updated, standardised and sufficiently detailed to support searches and business matching, particularly as artificial intelligence is increasingly used to analyse and connect data, he said. 
 
 Nguyen Thi Van Anh, chairwoman of Tam Nong Vietnam Cooperative, said the cooperative had introduced its purple rice products to the Australian market. 
 
 Previously, potential buyers had to contact the cooperative directly to obtain information. 
 
 “When customers want to learn about our products, they can now access information such as growing-area codes, production technology and product specifications directly on the digital platform before starting discussions and transactions,” she said. 
 
 Therefore,the platform goes beyond product promotion, giving international buyers digital access to Vietnamese suppliers and key information on product origin, quality, production and sustainability. 
 
 Extending trade beyond the exhibition 
 
 However, the Expo Platform is designed to complement rather than replace physical trade fairs. 
 
 While exhibitions allow buyers to inspect products, meet suppliers and visit production facilities, an online platform can keep company and product information available after an event ends. 
 
 Huynh Dinh Thai Linh, general director of WTC Becamex Co Ltd, said bringing professional buyers to production sites would allow companies to demonstrate their manufacturing processes, capacity and standards directly. 
 
 The approach is particularly relevant as overseas markets impose increasingly detailed requirements on product standards, traceability, sustainability and green production. 
 
 By combining digital product information with physical meetings and production-site visits, the Expo Platform provides another channel for Vietnamese businesses to maintain contact with international buyers and expand overseas market access./.

articles.title: US trade chief to consider trade deal tariff caps in excess capacity probe - Mining Weekly
articles.summary: US trade chief to consider trade deal tariff caps in excess capacity probe  Mining Weekly
articles.full_text:
MILWAUKEE - US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Tuesday that the Trump administration will take into consideration tariff caps negotiated in trade deals with countries as it weighs potential new duties in an investigation on excess industrial capacity.
Speaking to reporters ahead of a Group of 20 trade ministers meeting, Greer said he did not want to prejudge the outcome of a pending Section 301 investigation that is focused on excess capacity in China and other key trading partners.
"I don't want to get ahead of the report and proposed action, but I guess what I'll say on that is we value those deals, and we will certainly take them into account when we're looking at any outcomes of that report," Greer said.
"What I will say as well is that a lot of those deals, they actually, you know, as they're implemented, they go a long way to mitigating some of the impacts of excess capacity that might be present in those countries," Greer said after a roundtable of CEOs and trade ministers.
The Trump administration has used its presidency of the G20 summit process this year to bring attention to China's excess production capacity and over-reliance on exports for growth.
At the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, at the beginning of September, all G20 member countries except China agreed to take actions against such policies.
The European Union is among 16 economies targeted by the excess capacity probe, along with Japan and South Korea. USTR has cited large EU trade surpluses, particularly on chemicals, machinery and vehicles in Germany and pharmaceuticals in Ireland as potential evidence of excess capacity.
Trade deals struck with the Trump administration by the EU, Japan and South Korea have capped US tariffs on their goods at 15%, while largely eliminating tariffs on US industrial goods. Greer has previously said that "a deal's a deal" when asked whether the US would abide by those caps.
The excess capacity probe was launched in March after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad global tariffs imposed under a national emergencies law.
European Union trade chief Maros Sefcovic told the CEO roundtable on Tuesday he welcomed the Trump administration's focus on combating excess industrial capacity at the G20 meeting. He added that the EU was pushing for reforms on excess capacity in the G20 framework and at the World Trade Organization.
He also said the EU was working towards deeper cooperation with the US and other allies on critical minerals to secure supply chains and avoid "weaponization" of the materials, production of which is currently dominated by China.

articles.title: Vietnam’s agro-forestry-fishery exports rise 7.8% in nine months - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam’s agro-forestry-fishery exports rise 7.8% in nine months  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) - Vietnam’s agro-forestry-fishery exports maintained growth momentum in the first nine months of 2026 despite continued volatility in global markets, reaching 56.3 billion USD, up 7.8% year on year. The sector posted a trade surplus of 16.9 billion USD, an increase of 7.4%.
According to the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, agro-forestry-fishery exports in September alone were estimated at 6.51 billion USD, up 5.7% year on year.
In the January-September period, agricultural exports reached 29.28 billion USD, up 3.1%; seafood exports 9.17 billion USD, up 12.3%; and forestry exports 14.41 billion USD, up 7.6%. Shipments of livestock products surged 24.6% to 564.4 million USD.
By region, Asia was the largest export market for Vietnam's major agricultural, forestry and fishery products, accounting for 49.4% of the market share. The next two largest markets were the Americas and Europe, with respective market shares of 22.2% and 13.5%. Africa and Oceania accounted for smaller shares, at 2.3% and 1.5%, respectively.
Exports to Asia increased 11.9% year on year, while those to the Americas, Europe and Oceania rose 2.3%, 2.6% and 15.5%, respectively. Meanwhile, shipments to Africa fell 16.7%.
China, the US and Japan were the three largest individual markets, with respective shares of 24.4%, 19.8% and 7.4%. Exports to all three markets increased, with shipments to China posting particularly strong growth of 18.9%.
Fruit and vegetables remained a standout performer, with exports reaching nearly 7.35 billion USD, up 19.9%. China accounted for 63% of the total, followed by the US and the Republic of Korea.
Seafood exports also maintained double-digit growth, rising 12.3% to 9.17 billion USD. China, the US and Japan were the three biggest markets, accounting for 23.7%, 15.7% and 14%, respectively.
Among forestry products, wood and wooden products continued to play a leading role. In the first nine months of 2026, their exports reached nearly 13.43 billion USD, up 7.3% year on year. The US was the largest market, accounting for 50.1%, followed by China and Japan, with shares of 15% and 12.5%, respectively.
However, several major agricultural commodities faced pressure from lower prices or weaker demand.
In the first nine months, coffee exports rose 15.4% in volume to 1.4 million tonnes, but their value fell 7.3% to 6.54 billion USD as the average export price dropped 19.7% to 4,537.3 USD per tonne.
Rice exports also declined, falling 6.1% in volume to 6.4 million tonnes and 10.9% in value to 3.11 billion USD. The Philippines remained the largest market, accounting for 40.9% of the total, followed by China at 17.4% and Ghana at 12.7%. Notably, the value of rice exports to China surged 76% in the first eight months of the year.
Rubber exports fell 16.2% in volume and 4.4% in value to 1.1 million tonnes and 2.18 billion USD, respectively. However, the average export price rose 14.1% to 2,016.8 USD per tonne.
For tea, export volume fell 7.7%, but export value edged up 0.4% to 167.9 million USD, while the average export price increased by 8.7%. The higher price played an important role in offsetting part of the decline in export volume.
Several other agricultural products also continued to post positive results. In the first nine months, cashew nut exports reached 543,400 tonnes, worth 3.85 billion USD. Despite a 2% decline in volume, export value still rose by 2%, supported by a 4.2% increase in the average export price to 7,084.4 USD per tonne. China, the US and the Netherlands were the three largest markets.
Pepper recorded solid growth in both volume and value. Vietnam exported 214,400 tonnes of pepper worth 1.4 billion USD, up 15% and 10.2%, respectively. The US remained the largest market, accounting for 26.7% of the market share, followed by Germany and Thailand. Notably, export value to Thailand increased by 52.8%, while exports to Türkiye surged 97.7% among the 15 largest markets.
Meanwhile, the total value of agricultural, forestry and fishery imports in the first nine months was estimated at 39.4 billion USD, up 8% year on year. Of this, the imports of agricultural products were valued at 24.96 billion USD, up 11.3%; livestock products at 4 billion USD, up 21.4%; fishery products at 2.44 billion USD, up 0.6%; and forestry products at 2.81 billion USD, up 17%./.

articles.title: Vietnam’s manufacturing sector maintains growth in September: S&P Global - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam’s manufacturing sector maintains growth in September: S&P Global  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Vietnam’s manufacturing sector continued to grow in September, although rates of expansion in output and new orders eased from those seen in August, according to the Vietnam Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) report released by S&P Global on October 1.
The report showed that the Vietnam Manufacturing PMI fell to 51.9 in September from 53.3 in August, indicating a smaller improvement in the health of the sector at the end of the third quarter. Nonetheless, business conditions have strenghtened in each of the past 15 months.
A further marked rise in manufacturing production was registered in September, continuing the sequence of expansion which began in May 2025. However, the rate of growth eased from that seen in August.
Panellists reported that higher new orders were behind the latest increase in output, but the pace of expansion slowed.
Where new orders increased, panellists reported improving market conditions and customers expanding their order volumes. There were again reports of weakness in international demand, however, resulting in a second successive fall in new export orders. New business from abroad decreased solidly, and at the fastest pace since April. Backlogs of work were broadly unchanged in September, after having risen in each of the previous two months.
A further marked increase in purchasing activity was recorded in September as firms secured inputs to help support output growth. The use of materials in the production process meant that stocks of inputs continued to fall.
Manufacturers also expressed a desire to draw down holdings of finished products, and used the prompt shipment of goods to customers to achieve this.
In fact, stocks of finished goods decreased at the sharpest pace since the survey began in March 2011. Suppliers' delivery times lengthened modestly, meanwhile, with panellists linking delays to issues with international shipping and poor weather conditions.
International issues were also central to a further rise in input costs as the war in the Middle East caused higher prices for fuel and oil. Increased transportation costs were also reported.
The rate of input price inflation was marked and slightly faster than in August, albeit still among the lowest over the past year.
Andrew Harker, Economics Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence said that while Vietnamese manufacturing sector remained in growth territory in September, data showed that the international environment limited the pace of expansion.
New export orders were down, the war in the Middle East caused further rises in the cost of fuel and oil, and international shipping delays contributed to longer supplier delivery times.
Despite these headwinds, production continued to rise markedly, and firms were more optimistic in the outlook for the coming year, Harker said.
“Based on the historical relationship between the PMI and official data, the manufacturing sector should continue to make a solid contribution to GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026, with the potential for growth to strengthen further should the international environment improve,” he continued./.

articles.summary: Trade Chief Asks USTR Representative to Respect 15% Tariff Agreement at G20  news.sbs.co.kr
articles.full_text:
Park Jung-sung, Minister for Trade at the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, attended the Group of 20 (G20) Trade Ministers' Meeting held in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA, where he emphasized international cooperation to address global overproduction and stabilize supply chains.
According to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy today (the 2nd), Minister Park actively presented the South Korean government's position during discussions across four sessions held over two days starting from the 30th of last month: ▲ the weaponization of food, ▲ structural overproduction, ▲ most-favored-nation (MFN) reform, and ▲ the elimination of forced labor within global supply chains.
Regarding the issue of steel oversupply in particular, he emphasized, "It is important to adhere to basic principles such as voluntary corporate restructuring and trade remedies based on World Trade Organization (WTO) rules," adding that "it must not lead to overprotection that deviates from international norms."
Taking advantage of this multilateral meeting, Minister Park held bilateral talks with major countries including the United States, China, the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom, Japan, India, Türkiye, Australia, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Brazil to discuss pending trade issues.
Minister Park met with Jamieson Greer, the United States Trade Representative (USTR), to request respect for the 15% tariff agreement and agreed to coordinate a specific schedule for the South Korea-U.S. joint committee, now that the first project for investment in the U.S. has been announced.
With Maroš Šefčovič, EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, he discussed the legislative trends of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) and ways to resolve uncertainties for domestic companies.
In a meeting with Jonathan Reynolds, the UK Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills, he expressed gratitude for the UK's exemption of regional sanctions related to South Korea's imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
In addition, he solidified cooperation on critical minerals and energy supply chains with China, Australia, and Indonesia, while discussing the expansion of economic partnerships such as free trade agreements (FTAs) with emerging economies like Saudi Arabia and Brazil.

Coffee prices today, September 30, 2026
 World coffee prices showed mixed movements on the London and New York futures exchanges.
 Robusta coffee prices on the London exchange experienced slight downward pressure across all contract periods. Conversely, the New York exchange witnessed a positive surge in Arabica prices, reaching their highest level in 2.5 weeks. Although longer delivery contracts such as July 2027 and September 2027 saw slight declines of 0.3 to 0.4 cents/lb, the Arabica market generally remained in positive territory for closer contracts due to concerns about supply in South America.
 Coffee prices have cooled from their session highs, with robusta prices falling into negative territory after the Brazilian Real hit a six-week low against the US dollar. A weaker Real encourages Brazilian coffee producers to boost export sales. Prices are also under pressure from increased trade flows, but the market is in an oversold state, attracting renewed interest from investment funds.
 Meanwhile, in terms of market supply, Brazilian coffee exports are on track to set a record in September, with exports to date 34% higher than the same period last year. Brazil has essentially completed its record coffee harvest, however concerns about quality may lead to lower-than-expected actual supply.
 The volatile nature of arabica contracts on the ICE exchange in the US is making it more difficult to close significant deals. In recent weeks, the asking price on the Brazilian physical coffee market has fallen in line with the downward trend in New York prices. As a result, farmers are now only selling coffee on a daily basis, in quantities necessary to meet immediate payment obligations, which are high at the end of the harvest and processing of the new crop.”

 Domestic coffee prices fluctuated within a narrow range. After several sessions of back-and-forth adjustments, the purchase price in key purchasing areas remained at around 93,000 VND/kg. This price level helped farmers and dealers maintain confidence amidst the volatile international agricultural commodity markets.
 Analyzing the overall market, experts believe that the slight adjustment in domestic coffee prices stems from a localized supply shortage at the end of the season. The amount of old crop coffee held by farmers and trading companies has almost completely run out, forcing buyers to raise their purchase prices to fulfill previously signed export contracts. In addition, the persistently high USD/VND exchange rate also partly supports agricultural prices when converted into domestic currency.
 The biggest downward pressure on the domestic market currently comes from the upcoming harvest in the Central Highlands. With the abundant new supply entering the market, the upward trend in bulk coffee bean prices may be halted. However, the risk of unusual climate change affecting actual yields, along with high international logistics costs, will be important factors preventing a sharp drop in coffee prices, helping to maintain prices near historical peaks in the medium term.

AI making major splash in trade with ASEAN
Both sides aim to expand tech's role in bilateral commerce, which topped $1 trillion last year
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transitioning from a conceptual showcase to a practical driver of cross-border trade, reshaping the economic, industrial and digital integration between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Wei Qiaomei, a livestreamer, once struggled to grasp exactly what her Thai customers wanted, despite speaking fluent Thai. Ahead of a recent pitch for a portable fan, an AI system analyzed Thai e-commerce data and instantly provided her with two localized selling points: quiet motors and long battery life. The trial proved highly rewarding, with her employer, based in South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, reporting a 300 percent jump in sales.
Noting that speaking a language is not the same as understanding a market, the 23-year-old observed that AI had transformed her from a mere translator into a market-savvy presenter. Her company trained its model on ASEAN languages, local preferences and cultural nuances, enabling it to analyze products, process reviews and draft localized scripts, while livestreaming hosts decide when to pivot, how to handle tough questions and what to emphasize. For Wei, the technology did not replace her. Rather, it amplified her capabilities.
Wei's story reflects a broader, systemic shift in relations between China and ASEAN, as both sides aim to expand the role of AI in bilateral trade, which exceeded $1 trillion (7.1 trillion yuan) last year. In the first seven months this year, China-ASEAN trade rose 24.7 percent year-on-year to $744.41 billion, according to Chinese Customs data, driven by the expanding use of advanced computing in marketing, agriculture, logistics and finance. The distinction between technology that merely draws a crowd and technology that delivers tangible commercial value was the central focus of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and the China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit, held in Nanning, capital of Guangxi, in September.
The event brought together more than 3,400 companies across a total exhibition area of 170,000 square meters, with Timor-Leste attending for the first time as ASEAN's 11th member and an official co-host. The expo's inaugural "AI marketplace" and exclusive exhibition areas for ASEAN national market needs featured about 500 products from more than 70 companies across eight categories, including wearables, health management and consumer technology, allowing visitors to test and purchase items on-site.
Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat, said: "While AI was mostly for show last year, it is now actively propelling sales and becoming a new hot spot for regional economic and trade cooperation."
This transition from exhibition to execution is evident across multiple sectors and borders. In Laos and Cambodia, a platform developed by a Guangxi enterprise and local partners utilizes satellite imagery, drones and ground sensors to track pests and guide tropical crop cultivation.
Built with Chinese technology, local field data and training support, the system has been tested on more than 1,333 hectares of crops, said project head Wen Biaotang.
In Guangxi's border city of Chongzuo, the local center for disease control and prevention has partnered with neighboring Vietnamese provinces to deploy a bilingual platform for early disease detection, slashing epidemiological reporting times from four hours to just 30 minutes. Meanwhile, in Nanning, a platform named RunDo remotely monitors almost 300 megawatts of solar capacity across nearly 3,000 sites in Malaysia, replacing manual inspections with drones and intelligent algorithms.
The platform has boosted maintenance efficiency by over 30 percent, raised power output by up to 5 percent, and cut labor costs by more than 20 percent. Leveraging Nanning's computing infrastructure, ASEAN companies can avoid building large intelligent computing centers and remotely access models and computing power for their business needs, an approach that has already launched more than 80 computing projects across the region.
The demand for practical, industry-level solutions was highly palpable at the expo, where entities like Guangxi Publishing and Media Group and Maiyue Technology showcased their innovative applications to empower China-ASEAN digital industry cooperation.
During the event, Li Laiyou, chairman of Guangxi Publishing and Media Group, introduced an AI short drama co-creation platform. Launched in July 2026 by its subsidiary Flytoto Culture & Technology Co based in Nanning, the platform utilizes top-tier video generation technology to complete the entire production process — from scriptwriting to video generation, editing and dubbing. Since August, the group has produced over 100 AI short dramas, with about 40 already airing on major streaming platforms.
Designed as an open ecosystem, the AI short drama co-creation platform has attracted over 1,000 institutions and individual creators, including users from Malaysia and other ASEAN member states. Li said a local Southeast Asian film and television institution has already reached a strategic partnership with the group to jointly develop short dramas. This digital push builds upon the group's established physical presence in the region, which includes copyright export branches in Vietnam, Laos, Thailand and Malaysia, facilitating the export of about 400 book titles annually.
Over the next three to five years, the group plans to focus heavily on cross-border cooperation in the micro-drama sector. By partnering with leading overseas broadcasting platforms, it aims to export AI-generated content based on Chinese and foreign literary classics, using short dramas as a dynamic new medium to promote cultural exchange across ASEAN and beyond.
Similarly, Maiyue Technology, the official designated technical service provider for the expo, demonstrated the tangible impact of AI hardware across a massive 100-square-meter upgraded exhibition space. The company unveiled three new types of augmented reality and AI glasses — specifically designed for consumer translation, travel companionship and AR viewing.
These devices significantly expand language coverage and recognition accuracy, breaking traditional language barriers for cross-border exhibitions, tourism and daily life. The real-time, high-precision translation capabilities even drew the attention of prominent livestreamers, echoing the growing reliance on AI tools in digital commerce.
Beyond consumer hardware, Maiyue showcased its intelligent platform foundation and AI computing power all-in-one machines, presenting full-track solutions for education, government affairs, cultural tourism and aviation.
Furthermore, Maiyue launched five new products covering computing security, AR real-scene applications, simultaneous conference interpretation and cross-border payments. By providing self-service AI translation glasses rentals at the venue and supporting high-level forums with zero-latency translation systems, the company directly addressed ASEAN's diverse digital transformation needs.
To further anchor its regional presence, the newly opened Maiyue technology park exhibition hall hosted numerous overseas delegations and research teams, serving as a vital offline hub for linking China's AI scientific and technological strengths with ASEAN's digital cooperation.
The physical connectivity of the region is already undergoing a historic transformation. The full navigation of the Pinglu Canal has drastically shortened the inland shipping distance from China's southwestern hinterland to ASEAN markets, opening up a bidirectional economic corridor. Just as the canal bridges physical distances, spatial intelligence technologies are shortening the industrial distance of digitalizing the physical world from merely being visible to being practically usable.
Yang Yanyan, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit Secretariat, emphasized that the accelerated construction of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 version has comprehensively launched cooperation in nine major areas, including the digital economy, the green economy, and the interconnectivity of industrial and supply chains.
Over its 22-year history in Nanning, the summit has held more than 200 economic and trade activities, effectively serving as an amplifier for government-business dialogue, a multiplier for economic cooperation and an optimizer for the business environment.
However, these cross-border deployments highlight strict prerequisites: computing power, local data, skilled workers and capable local partners. Guangxi's China-ASEAN artificial intelligence application cooperation center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential scenarios, opened 279 to developers, and set up offices in Vietnam, Laos and Malaysia, backed more than 30 cross-border projects, and assembled an alliance of 55 companies.
To address the low-resource challenge faced by some Southeast Asian languages, a training base in Malaysia has logged more than 1,900 hours of multilingual data annotation, while a regional competition attracted more than 200 teams.
Liu Jianmin, a professor at the School of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence of Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, said ASEAN universities, companies and professionals must contribute to collecting, labeling and updating data if models are to work locally, warning that no matter how accurate a system is, if no one uses it, can afford it or can keep it running, it remains just an exhibit.

articles.title: From tariffs to triumph - The Financial Express
articles.summary: From tariffs to triumph  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
The recent decision of the United States (US) government to impose a 37 per cent 'discounted reciprocal tariff' on Bangladeshi exports has reverberated with shock through the country's business and policy circles. As per a chart published by the White House, Bangladesh is reported to levy an effective 74 per cent tariff on American goods, ranking it among the highest US trading partners.
This development, part of Trump's "Liberation Day" trade policy, aims to counter what the administration describes as unfair trade practices and protectionist barriers against American exports. Under the new framework, the US has introduced a baseline 10 per cent tariff on all imports, with significantly higher rates for countries accused of currency manipulation or high trade barriers.
This poses a serious challenge for Bangladesh. The US is our single largest export destination, particularly for the RMG sector, which contributes more than 80 per cent of total exports. A 37 per cent tariff could significantly erode our competitive edge, especially as key competitors like India (26 per cent), Pakistan (29 per cent), and Vietnam (46 per cent) face varying but comparatively lower tariff rates.
To effectively tackle this challenge, Bangladesh must adopt a proactive, strategic approach. This involves leveraging both diplomacy and trade policy adjustments to mitigate risks and enhance economic ties with the US.
A key step in this strategy would be to revisit tariff structures on US imports to create room for negotiation. Currently, Bangladesh imposes a 5 per cent Advance Income Tax (AIT) on US raw cotton, a critical input for the textile industry. Reducing this tax to zero per cent -while simultaneously seeking duty-free access for garments manufactured using US cotton-could be a pragmatic move.
This approach, if successful, could lead to a win-win situation. US exporters, especially cotton producers, would gain a larger, more reliable market in Bangladesh. Bangladeshi apparel manufacturers, already grappling with high production costs, would regain a competitive edge in the US market, fostering a sense of hope and optimism.
Additionally, Bangladesh already offers zero duty on aircraft parts and 5 per cent on scrap metals, with low tariffs on LPG and energy imports. Extending a zero-duty framework to key US exports-such as cotton and high-tech equipment-could position Bangladesh as a priority partner under the US "reciprocal tariff" doctrine.
Trade policies are rarely set in stone, and diplomacy plays a crucial role in shaping tariff negotiations. To counteract the new tariff structure, Bangladesh must: (a) initiate immediate diplomatic engagements with US trade representatives to argue for a fairer framework; (b) strengthen bilateral trade cooperation by highlighting Bangladesh's contributions to the US supply chain; (c) leverage regional alliances-especially within South Asia-to advocate for more balanced US trade policies; and (d) explore alternative trade routes and diversify export markets to reduce over-reliance on the US market.
While the 37 per cent tariff poses a significant challenge, it also presents an opportunity to reshape Bangladesh-US trade relations. If approached strategically, this moment could lead to a more balanced, resilient, and sustainable trade framework, securing long-term economic stability for Bangladesh.
In times of adversity lie opportunities. Now is the time for decisive, creative, and courageous action.
Md. Sahidul Islam is Head of Business, Corporate Head Office, Shimanto Bank PLC. sahidul.islam@shimantobank.com

On the afternoon of September 30th, the Ministry of Industry and Trade held a conference to review the tasks of the third quarter and September; and to implement the tasks for October and the direction of tasks for the fourth quarter of 2026.
The conference was held in person at the Ministry of Industry and Trade headquarters, chaired by Minister Le Manh Hung, with the participation of Deputy Ministers Luong Hoang Thai and Nguyen Viet Son, and leaders of departments, divisions, and units under the Ministry, as well as a number of businesses and corporations; it was also connected online to the Departments of Industry and Trade of provinces and cities and the system of Vietnamese trade offices abroad.
6 out of 8 targets were met or exceeded.
Presenting a summary report on the implementation of tasks in September and the first nine months of 2026, Director of the Planning and Finance Department Bui Huy Son stated that, according to Resolution No. 01/NQ-CP, the Ministry of Industry and Trade was assigned eight growth targets.
By the end of the first nine months of 2026, six out of eight targets had been met or exceeded, including three targets that were exceeded and three that were met (exports increased by 24.0%, exceeding the nine-month plan by 7.3 percentage points; total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue increased by approximately 13.1-13.6%, within the annual target range; Industrial Production Index (IIP) increased by 12.1-12.2%, basically adhering to the scenario; total electricity production and import increased by 9.5%; the power reserve ratio reached 26.3% and the percentage of businesses applying e-commerce reached 68%, both exceeding the targets).
However, two targets have not yet been met and need to be prioritized for monitoring in the fourth quarter: total power generation capacity increased by approximately 3.5% in the first nine months, lower than the minimum target of 6.6%, with the possibility of achieving this largely depending on the progress of bringing new power generation projects into operation; and B2C e-commerce market growth reached 19.5%, still lower than the target of 20-22%.
According to Director Bui Huy Son, in addition to quantitative indicators, the trade balance shifted to a deficit of $21.83 billion, with imports increasing faster than exports.
“ Overall, industrial production, exports, and the domestic market continue to maintain positive growth momentum, with most indicators meeting or exceeding targets. However, there is still limited room for maneuver; issues related to power generation capacity, export growth quality, trade deficit, energy prices, and international financial fluctuations need to be closely monitored in the fourth quarter,” Director Bui Huy Son informed.
Prioritize removing obstacles to processing and manufacturing.
Regarding the industrial production and trade situation of the sector, according to Director Bui Huy Son, after 9 months of 2026, production, trade and energy activities generally maintained a positive trend, but the level of recovery and quality of growth among sectors remained differentiated, and some structural risks emerged that need to be proactively managed in the remaining months of the year.
Firstly, industrial production continued to maintain double-digit growth and basically followed the planned scenario. The Industrial Production Index (IIP) for the first nine months increased by 12.1-12.2%, but growth was uneven across sectors and localities.
Secondly, the domestic market continues to be the backbone of growth, with total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue increasing by approximately 13.1-13.6%.

Thirdly, exports increased sharply by 24.0%, continuing to be a prominent driving force, but the quality of growth was uneven. The FDI sector accounted for 80.9% of total export turnover and increased by 29.2%, while the domestic enterprise sector only increased by 6.1%.
Fourth , imports and the trade balance continue to reflect both positive aspects and structural risks. Imports increased by 36.9%, 12.9 percentage points higher than exports; the trade balance showed a deficit of US$21.83 billion. The focus in the fourth quarter needs to shift strongly from expanding participation to improving transaction efficiency, service quality, and digital platform management capabilities.
In the final months of the year, to achieve the highest possible results for 2026, Director Bui Huy Son stated that the Ministry of Industry and Trade prioritizes focusing on the following groups of solutions:
Firstly, for industrial production, review each sector and locality where growth is lower than projected, quantify the shortfall and potential contribution in the fourth quarter; prioritize removing obstacles for processing, manufacturing, orders, raw materials, and projects capable of generating additional output within the year.
Secondly , regarding electricity and energy, accelerate the progress of key power generation and transmission projects; develop electricity supply plans based on load scenarios; and ensure fuel and reserves.

articles.title: RBI FEMA Export-Import Amendments Now in Effect: Key Changes for Businesses - india-briefing.com
articles.summary: RBI FEMA Export-Import Amendments Now in Effect: Key Changes for Businesses  india-briefing.com
articles.full_text:
The Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, are now in force from 1 October 2026. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has introduced changes in FEMA to prescribed periods under Regulation 5, transitional treatment for exporters on the Caution List, and the handling of certain legacy export, import, and merchanting trade transactions by Authorised Dealers.
The changes are relevant to businesses engaged in cross-border trade and to Authorised Dealers responsible for processing foreign-exchange transactions.
Manage Trade Compliance
We support importers and exporters with registrations, FEMA compliances, product classification, and recurring filings.
What has changed for exporters under the 2026 FEMA amendments?
The amendments now in force introduce three key changes:
- Specified periods under Regulation 5 have been shortened
- Exporters who were on the Caution List as of 30 September 2026 remain subject to their existing RBI orders until they are removed from the list
- Authorised dealers can handle specified transactions undertaken before 1 October 2026, where such transactions previously required RBI approval under the earlier FEMA framework
These provisions establish the compliance framework now applicable to businesses following the commencement of the amended regulations.
Regulation 5: Export proceeds must be realised within shorter periods
The FEMA amended Regulation 5(1) reduces the prescribed period for realisation and repatriation of export proceeds. The amendment replaces the existing 15-month period with nine months under clauses (a) and (b). It also reduces the period specified in the first proviso from 18 months to 12 months.
In practice, under the amended framework, the general period for realising and repatriating export proceeds is nine months, with the applicable starting point depending on the type of export. For goods, the period runs from the date of shipment, while for services it runs from the date of invoice. Goods exported to an overseas warehouse are subject to a nine-month period from the date of sale from the warehouse. Exports invoiced and/or settled in Indian rupees are subject to the 12-month period specified in the first proviso.
CLICK HERE: Import-Export Procedures in India: 2026 Edition
Caution list: Existing RBI orders continue to apply
The amended FEMA Regulation 13 provides transitional treatment for exporters who were already on the Caution List immediately before 1 October 2026.
Exporters who were on the Caution List as of 30 September 2026, under RBI orders issued pursuant to Regulation 16 of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015, continue to be governed by those orders until they are removed from the Caution List.
The Caution List is an RBI mechanism used to subject certain exporters to closer regulatory oversight, particularly where export proceeds remain unrealised or outstanding beyond the prescribed period. An exporter placed on the Caution List may face additional conditions or restrictions when undertaking further export transactions, with authorised dealers required to follow the applicable RBI directions when processing such transactions.
Authorised dealers can handle specified legacy transactions
The amended regulations introduce Regulation 20, “Powers to Authorised Dealers.”
The provision enables authorised dealers to handle specified transactions involving export and import of goods, services and merchanting trade, where the transactions were undertaken before 1 October 2026 and previously required RBI approval under the earlier FEMA framework.
This covers transactions governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015, and relevant RBI Master Directions on the export and import of goods and services.
What this means for businesses
Companies with outstanding pre-October 1 transactions should identify cases where RBI approval was previously required and assess whether the transaction now falls within Regulation 20.
Where applicable, businesses can work with their Authorised Dealers to process such transactions under the new provision.
Importantly, Regulation 20 concerns specified legacy transactions undertaken before 1 October 2026. It does not constitute a blanket removal of RBI approval requirements for transactions undertaken on or after 1 October.
ALSO READ: New FEMA Non-Debt Rules: Impact on Individual Foreign Investors
Compliance actions for businesses affected by the 2026 FEMA amendments
With the amended regulations now in force, businesses should implement the provisions relevant to their cross-border transactions.
Exporters: Review FEMA Regulation 5 timelines
Exporters should review transactions covered by Regulation 5 and apply the revised nine-month and 12-month periods for realisation and repatriation of export proceeds, as applicable. Internal compliance calendars and receivables-monitoring systems should be updated accordingly.
Businesses with legacy transactions: Review outstanding cases
Businesses involved in the export or import of goods, export or import of services, or merchanting trade should identify transactions undertaken before 1 October 2026 that remain pending or require regulatory action.
Where a transaction previously required RBI approval, the business should consult its authorised dealer to determine whether Regulation 20 now permits the Authorised Dealer to handle the transaction.
Exporters on the caution list: Continue existing obligations
Exporters who were on the Caution List as of 30 September 2026 should continue complying with the applicable RBI orders until they are removed from the list.
Finance, treasury, trade, and compliance teams: Update procedures for FEMA export and import regulations
Companies affected by these provisions should update their FEMA compliance processes to reflect:
- Revised Regulation 5 periods for applicable export transactions
- Continuing obligations under existing caution list orders
- The Authorised Dealer’s ability to handle specified pre-October 1 legacy transactions
This distinction is important because Regulation 5 primarily affects exporters; the Caution List provision applies specifically to exporters already on the list, while Regulation 20 can affect businesses involved in exports, imports, services, and merchanting trade with qualifying pre-October 1 transactions.

articles.title: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners? - Yahoo News Singapore
articles.summary: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners?  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.
Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.
A trade order under strain
The EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.
Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."
Related
The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.
But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."
The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.
What each side wants
For the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence.
"We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.
For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.
Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.
The rule-taker question
The hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.
Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.
Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.
Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.
Related
Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.
The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.
Limits and risks
The idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.
Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.
Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

Upgraded Forecast Signals Confidence
S&P Global Ratings has revised Vietnam's economic growth projection upward to 8 per cent for 2026, marking a significant upgrade from earlier estimates and positioning the country among the fastest-expanding economies in Southeast Asia. The revision comes as part of a broader assessment that sees the Asia-Pacific region maintaining momentum despite global headwinds.
The ratings agency attributes the stronger outlook to Vietnam's improving domestic consumption patterns, sustained export competitiveness in electronics and textiles, and continued foreign direct investment inflows into manufacturing hubs. Data from Vietnam's General Statistics Office shows industrial production expanding at double-digit rates through the third quarter, with electronics assembly and garment exports driving much of the acceleration.
S&P's assessment also highlights Vietnam's stabilising inflation environment, which has allowed the State Bank of Vietnam to maintain accommodative monetary policy settings without triggering currency volatility. Consumer price inflation has averaged below 4 per cent year-on-year through September, giving policymakers room to support credit growth in priority sectors.
Regional Context
The upgraded Vietnam forecast sits within S&P's broader view that Asia-Pacific growth will remain resilient in 2026, supported by intra-regional trade flows and investment in digital infrastructure. The agency projects regional expansion at approximately 4.5 per cent, with Southeast Asian economies outperforming developed markets in Northeast Asia.
Vietnam's trajectory mirrors patterns seen in Indonesia and the Philippines, where domestic consumption and manufacturing investment are offsetting slower demand from traditional export markets in Europe and North America. Trade data shows Vietnam's exports to other ASEAN members and India rising by more than 12 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, partially compensating for softer shipments to the United States.
The ratings agency notes that Vietnam's current account surplus has widened to an estimated 2.8 per cent of GDP, providing a buffer against external shocks and supporting the dong's stability. Foreign exchange reserves have climbed above five months of import cover, the highest level in three years.
Structural Challenges Remain
S&P's report acknowledges that Vietnam faces structural constraints that could moderate growth beyond the near term. These include an underdeveloped domestic capital market, limited high-value manufacturing capabilities, and infrastructure bottlenecks in power generation and logistics networks.
The agency points to Vietnam's reliance on foreign-invested enterprises for approximately 70 per cent of export value, a concentration that leaves growth vulnerable to shifts in global supply-chain strategies. Domestic firms remain smaller and less integrated into international production networks, limiting spillover benefits from FDI.
Banking sector asset quality is another area S&P flags for monitoring. Non-performing loan ratios have declined but remain elevated in real estate and construction lending, where developers face refinancing pressures amid tighter credit conditions. The agency estimates that restructured loans, not classified as NPLs, could add another two to three percentage points to reported figures.
What Comes Next
S&P's outlook for Vietnam hinges on the government's ability to accelerate public investment disbursement in the fourth quarter and into 2027. Infrastructure projects financed by official development assistance and concessional loans have lagged, with execution rates below 50 per cent of allocated budgets in some ministries.
The agency also emphasises the importance of continued regulatory reforms to attract higher-value manufacturing and technology investment. Vietnam has committed to implementing intellectual property protections and reducing administrative barriers as part of trade agreements, but progress has been uneven across provinces.
Regional developments will shape Vietnam's trajectory. Any escalation in trade tensions affecting electronics supply chains or disruptions to shipping routes through the South China Sea could dampen export growth. Conversely, further diversification of production out of China could accelerate FDI inflows into Vietnamese manufacturing zones.
S&P expects to review its forecast again in early 2027, once full-year fiscal data and fourth-quarter trade figures are available. The agency maintains a stable outlook on Vietnam's sovereign credit rating, reflecting confidence in the country's external buffers and policy flexibility.

articles.title: Singapore studies fusion as potential clean-energy pathway - Singapore Business Review
articles.summary: Singapore studies fusion as potential clean-energy pathway  Singapore Business Review
articles.full_text:
Gov’t studying fusion as potential clean-energy pathway
The METI places greater emphasis on energy security, economic growth and climate resilience.
Singapore is studying nuclear fusion as a potential low-carbon energy pathway as the new Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) places greater emphasis on energy security, economic growth and climate resilience.
The Ministry of Trade and Industry formally became METI on 1 October, reflecting the growing importance of energy to Singapore’s economic competitiveness and long-term resilience.
Speaking at FusionX 2026, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng said energy was an essential resource requiring long-term planning.
He said global developments had strengthened the need for Singapore to study emerging energy technologies and leave no potential pathway unexplored.
Fusion energy is one option the country is monitoring closely, although commercially operating fusion power plants could still be years away. Singapore has not decided whether to deploy any form of nuclear energy.
Fusion generates energy by combining atomic nuclei under extreme heat and pressure, unlike nuclear fission, which splits atoms.
The technology could produce lower levels of radioactive waste and has a limited risk of runaway reactions, but maintaining stable fusion conditions and achieving a net-positive energy return remain major technical challenges.
Singapore’s exploration of fusion forms part of its wider effort to diversify its energy sources and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.
The country has increased its solar deployment target to 3 gigawatt-peak by 2030 after reaching its previous 2 GWp target ahead of schedule. It is also pursuing regional low-carbon electricity imports and studying the possible deployment of nuclear fission.
Singapore will participate in the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2027 to assess its readiness to make an informed decision on nuclear fission.
Even without constructing a fusion reactor, Singapore could participate in the industry through its expertise in precision engineering, advanced manufacturing, plasma diagnostics and deep technology.
A*STAR has worked with US-based Realta Fusion since 2025 to develop a diagnostic tool that measures plasma velocities, helping researchers understand and control conditions within fusion systems.
The agency and Realta Fusion are exploring further collaboration in advanced plasma diagnostics and deployment.
SGInnovate and consulting firm Helixos have identified materials and coatings, plasma-facing components, diagnostics, software and control systems as potential areas for Singapore to enter the global fusion value chain.

They said sympathy for the former Umno president should not overshadow the court’s decision or gloss over the weak checks and balances in place during the party’s time in government.
“Umno can support Najib’s pardon as a constitutional and humanitarian process, but it should not portray it as erasing or negating his conviction,” Universiti Malaya’s Tawfik Yaakub told FMT.
However, he said support for Najib as an individual must not be conflated with defending wrongdoings committed while in office.
Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC funds.
He was sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, former king Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah exercised his pardon powers by halving Najib’s jail term and reducing his fine to RM50 million.
Then, on Sept 18 this year, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of the fine and compliance with other stipulated conditions.
Umno subsequently set up a fund to help its former president to pay the fine, with party leaders, members and supporters encouraged to contribute voluntarily.
However, Tawfik said the issue ran much deeper, and that Umno must consider the wider impact of the case on the public and the country’s reputation.
He said the party must make clear that no public funds were being used, while ensuring that efforts to recover assets, pursue compensation and advance governance reforms continue.
“Umno does not automatically bear responsibility for an individual’s wrongdoing.
“However, as the party that led the government when the scandal erupted, Umno must acknowledge—in political and moral terms—that there were weaknesses in checks and balances at the time which cannot be repeated,” he said.
Tawfik said several reforms are urgently needed, including strengthening independent enforcement, ensuring transparency in political financing, mandating asset declarations, and tightening oversight of government-linked companies.
He said a clear separation between the interests of the party, the government and state institutions was also important to prevent such problems from recurring.
Meanwhile, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia’s Mazlan Ali said Umno’s “culture and governance” had changed little since Barisan Nasional’s defeat in the 14th general election.
“The party still follows its old ways,” he said.
However, Mazlan noted that Umno’s role in Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government had, to some extent, compelled the party to adapt to a political climate that places greater emphasis on transparency and integrity.
He said the Najib issue also highlighted differences in perception between some Umno supporters and other groups of voters.
Some rural Malays, Felda settlers, and Umno members and supporters viewed assistance for Najib as an act of solidarity and in humanitarian terms, said Mazlan.
In contrast, he said, many urban Malay, middle-class and non-Malay voters viewed Najib’s sentence as justified, given that the offences were established by the court.
Mazlan said that, to his knowledge, Khairy Jamaluddin was among the few prominent Umno figures to have openly acknowledged the wrongdoing and harm the case had caused the country.
However, he admitted that many Umno leaders continue to defend Najib, viewing him as a victim.
